title: "Mini-Project #01: What We Watched"

### Introduction

### Data Acquisition and Cleaning

```{r}
#' Acquire Netflix What We Watched Reports
#' 
#' This function will acquire and standardize all data for MP#01
#' from Netflix. Because Netflix hosts the data files behind a CDN, we
#' are accessing the release pages and automatically extracting links to the
#' relevant files (with CDN hash). 
#' 
#' After import, files are stacked vertically and some basic cleaning is
#' performed. 
load_netflix_data <- function(){
  # Note to students: Make sure you have installed the tidyverse and fs packages
  #                   before beginning this assignment. If you aren't sure,
  #                   simply run `library(tidyverse)` at your R Console and, if
  #                   you don't see an error message, `tidyverse` has been 
  #                   installed. (Same for `fs`) If you still need to install
  #                   either package, use the `install.packages` function as 
  #                   demonstrated in class.
  library(tidyverse)
  library(rvest)
  library(readxl)
  library(fs)
  
  data_dir <- path("data", "mp01")
    
  if(!dir_exists(data_dir)){
    dir_create(data_dir, showWarnings=FALSE, recurse=TRUE)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS <- list(
    `2023H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-a-netflix-engagement-report",
    `2023H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2023",
    `2024H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2024",
    `2024H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2024",
    `2025H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2025",
    `2025H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2025",
    `2026H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2026"
  )
  
  download_if_needed <- function(url, local){
    if(!file_exists(local)){
      download.file(url, local, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb")
    }
    
    return(local)
  }
    
  NETFLIX_URLS |> 
    map(read_html) |> 
    map(html_element, xpath = "//a[contains(@href, '.xlsx')]") |> 
    map_chr(html_attr, "href") |> 
    enframe("period", "url") |> 
   mutate(path = path(data_dir, paste0(period, ".xlsx")), 
          path = map2(url, path, download_if_needed), 
          data = map(path, read_excel, skip=3, na="*"), 
          data = map(data, \(x) x |> mutate(`Release Date` = as.Date(`Release Date`)))) |>
    unnest(data) |> 
    select(-url, -path) |> 
    mutate(year=str_sub(period, 1, 4), 
           half=str_sub(period, start=6), 
           period_start = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 1, 7), 1), 
           period_end = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 7, 12), if_else(half==1, 30, 31))) |> 
    filter(!is.na(`Hours Viewed`)) |> 
    mutate(live_event = !is.na(Runtime) & str_detect(Runtime, "\\d+:\\d+\\*"), 
           clean_time = str_remove(Runtime, fixed("*")),
           Runtime = 60 * hour(hm(clean_time)) + minute(hm(clean_time))) |>
    select(-clean_time) |>
    mutate(Runtime = coalesce(Runtime, mean(Runtime, na.rm=TRUE)), 
           .by=Title, 
           Title = stringi::stri_trans_general(Title, "Latin-ASCII"),
           Title = str_remove(Title, " // .*"), 
           Title = str_remove(Title, "[^[:ascii:]].*"), 
           Title = str_trim(Title)) |>
    filter_out(Title == "") |>
    select(year, 
           period, 
           period_start, 
           period_end, 
           Title, 
           -half, 
           Runtime, 
           Views, 
           `Hours Viewed`, 
           `Release Date`,
           `Available Globally?`, 
           live_event)|>
rename(title = Title,
       runtime = Runtime,
       views = Views,
       hours_viewed = `Hours Viewed`,
       release_date = `Release Date`,
       available_globally =  `Available Globally?`)|>
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(year),
    available_globally =available_globally == "Yes"
  )
}

NETFLIX_DATA <- load_netflix_data()
```
### Initial Data Exploration

```{r}
library(skimr)
glimpse(NETFLIX_DATA)
```

```{r}
skim(NETFLIX_DATA)
```

After reviewing the data summary, we see we have 11 columns, 61,892 rows that contains a title viewership in a 6 month period, and the columns have the correct type now that we cleaned them. We can also see that we can rely more on the `year` and `hours_viewed` because there are no missing cells there, versus `runtime` (around 21% missing) and `views` (almost 30% missing), where we have some data missing. We can also see that we can rely on the data from `period_start` and `period_end` since there are also no missing values there compared to `release_date` where we have 35,251 missing cells and only 43% complete. Also, both `available_globally` and `live_event` are pretty reliable since only 2 rows are missing in `available_globally`. Having clarity on the above will help us make sure we are relying on complete data to make our analysis more accurate.

### Exploratory questions

```{r}
library(scales)
```

**1. What date range is covered by this data set?**

```{r}
#Date range
first_date <- min(NETFLIX_DATA$period_start)
last_date  <- max(NETFLIX_DATA$period_end)

```

The date range goes from `r first_date` until `r last_date`. 

**2. How many different shows and movies are covered in this data set?**

```{r}

#Number of distinct titles

n_titles <- n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$title)
```

There are `r comma(n_titles)` shows and movies covered in this data.

**3. How many total hours have been spent watching shows from the Bridgerton universe?**

```{r}
bridgerton_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Bridgerton")) |>
  summarize(total = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(total)
```

There have been `r comma(bridgerton_hours)` hours watched of Bridgerton universe during the date range described in the answer above for question number 1. 

**4. How many total hours have been spent watching the five seasons of Stranger Things? For this question, we only want the “real” Stranger Things shows and not the companion behind-the-scenes show (“Beyond Stranger Things”), the animated spin-off (“Tales from ’85”), or the background music (“Stranger Things: Fireplace”).**

```{r}
stranger_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Stranger Things")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Beyond Stranger Things")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Tales")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Stranger Things: Fireplace")) |>
  summarize(total = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(total)
```

The total amount of hours spent watching Stranger Things seasons 1 to 5 without including Beyond Stranger Things, Tales from ’85, and Stranger Things: Fireplace is `r comma(stranger_hours)`.

**5. What percentage of total watch time was spent on the Top 10 titles of 2026H1?**

```{r}
#share of 2026H1 watch time captured by the Top 10 titles
h1_2026 <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(period == "2026H1")

# Total includes all viewing, including the "Other Shows" aggregate
total_2026 <- sum(h1_2026$hours_viewed)

# Rank real titles only: "Other Shows" is an aggregate, not a single title
top10_2026 <- h1_2026 |>
  filter_out(title == "Other Shows") |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 10) |>
  summarize(total = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(total)

top10_share <- top10_2026 / total_2026
```

The percentage of total watch time spent on the top 10 titles of 2026H1 was `r percent(top10_share, accuracy = 0.1)`.

**6. What fraction of Netflix’s catalog is globally available? (Answer this both by title and weighted by hours viewed)**

```{r}
# Share of the catalog that is globally available

# By title: count each title once, then take the share that is global
global_by_title <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  distinct(title, available_globally) |>
  summarize(share = mean(available_globally, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull(share)

# Weighted by hours: share of all watch time that went to global titles
global_by_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarize(share = sum(hours_viewed[available_globally], na.rm = TRUE) /
                    sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(share)
```

The fraction of Netflix's catalog available globally by title is `r percent(global_by_title, accuracy = 0.1)`. The fraction available globally weighted by hours viewed is `r percent(global_by_hours, accuracy = 0.1)`. This means less than a fourth are available globally and those same titles are the ones that have more than half of the watch time.



### Corporate Strategy Memo
Write a brief (no more than 750 words) corporate strategy memo addressed to Netflix leadership. Your memo should help inform Netflix’s original content strategy for 2027 and beyond.

You can use the calculations performed above - or something similar - to include specific numerical evidence in support of your recommendations. For example, you should not say “live events are an increasingly large share of viewership” and should instead prefer a more specific claim like “live events have risen from X% to Y% of total watch time.”

Your memo should touch on at least 2 of the following possible topics:

Globally available vs. regionally licensed content
TV shows vs. movies
‘Big hits’ vs. the long-tail of smaller titles
Shorter ‘bite sized’ vs. longer content
‘Burstiness’ of viewership: do titles have a rush of viewership immediately after release (to partially answer this, you can use the period end and release date columns to get a “days available” value; combine this with a focus on titles that release near a period end)
Trends over time: identify time changes in the data, don’t simply aggregate 2023 to the present.
You may also address other structure or trends in the data you find interesting.
